question: Can the edge-level circuit-finding stage of mechanistic interpretability be automated by greedily activation-patching a transformer's computational graph, and can the resulting sparse subgraphs recover previously reported or exactly known circuits without admitting irrelevant components?

key_findings.claim: The paper's main conceptual contribution is a three-step circuit-analysis workflow, but ACDC automates only the pruning/search step rather than behavior selection, graph abstraction, or semantic interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: The workflow asks a researcher to select a behavior, dataset, and metric; choose the computational graph's granularity; and iteratively patch away unnecessary components. ACDC is explicitly scoped to automating step 3. The conclusion still requires practitioners to vary tasks and inspect the returned components to understand an algorithm.

key_findings.claim: ACDC is a greedy, reverse-topological edge deletion algorithm whose output is conditional on a clean/corrupted prompt pairing, a patching rule, a metric, a threshold, and parent traversal order.
key_findings.evidence: For each edge entering each node, ACDC tentatively deletes the edge, patches it with the activation from a corrupted input, and keeps the deletion when the increment in mean KL divergence from the full model is below threshold tau. Deletions are permanent, and the paper identifies parent ordering as a hyperparameter that changed the induction result.

anchors.section: J. Induction task: details and qualitative evidence

key_findings.claim: On the paper's main corrupted-activation, KL-based edge-recovery comparison, ACDC has the best AUC of the three methods on Docstring, Greater-Than, and IOI, but the ranking reverses under several equally plausible design choices.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 reports edge AUCs of 0.982/0.853/0.869 for ACDC on Docstring/Greater-Than/IOI, versus 0.805/0.693/0.789 for HISP and 0.937/0.806/0.823 for SP. With task-specific loss, however, ACDC falls to 0.461 on Greater-Than and 0.589 on IOI, below both or one of the alternatives. With zero ablation, ACDC's IOI KL edge AUC is 0.539 versus HISP's 0.792.

anchors.section: 4.1. Grounded in previous work: area under ROC curves

key_findings.claim: The strongest exact-recovery result occurs on tiny Tracr-compiled transformers and requires zero ablation plus a special corruption of positional embeddings.
key_findings.evidence: ACDC obtains edge AUC 1.000 on both the 10-edge tracr-xproportion and 15-edge tracr-reverse circuits with zero ablation, including a neuron-level exact graph. Under the corrupted-activation main setup the Tracr recovery is poor, and the implementation randomizes positional embeddings in corrupted examples so position-only components can be recovered.

anchors.section: I. Tracr tasks: details and qualitative evidence

key_findings.claim: ACDC can recover compact subgraphs overlapping manual circuits, but fidelity, sparsity, and agreement with the manual reference do not coincide.
key_findings.evidence: For Greater-Than, the abstract reports a 68-edge subgraph from roughly 32,000 GPT-2 Small edges that recovers all five manually identified component types. On Docstring, a 34-edge circuit close to the 37-edge manual graph has KL 1.2 and mean logit difference -1.7; lowering tau yields 258 edges with much better KL 0.33 and logit difference 0.58. The manual 37-edge graph itself has KL 1.1 and logit difference -1.6, showing that the reference circuit is also an imperfect behavioral target.

anchors.section: G. Greater-Than task: details and qualitative evidence

key_findings.claim: Single-metric discovery systematically mishandles components that reduce the chosen task score yet participate in the model's computation.
key_findings.evidence: The normal-threshold IOI run returns nine heads, all within the 26-head manual circuit, but misses negative name mover and previous-token heads. A lower threshold recovers those classes while also introducing undocumented heads. The paper explains that optimizing only logit difference or KL can omit behavior-harming 'negative' components by construction.

anchors.section: 4.1. Limitations of ROC ground truth and single metrics
F.3. Limitations of ACDC in recovering the IOI circuit

key_findings.claim: Reset-network controls provide useful evidence against pure sparsity artifacts, but they do not validate the semantic correctness or completeness of a discovered circuit.
key_findings.evidence: For induction, all methods produce substantially lower KL on the trained model than on weight-permuted reset networks, while HISP and SP can still optimize the reset model to some extent. This tests whether a method can hallucinate a performant subgraph when the learned behavior is disrupted, but it does not establish that surviving edges implement the human-described algorithm.

anchors.section: 4.2. Stand-alone circuit properties with a test metric

key_findings.claim: Greedy marginal deletion fails on redundant nonlinear computation even in a minimal OR-gate example.
key_findings.evidence: When two attention heads are interchangeable inputs to an OR gate, ACDC deletes the first tested input and keeps only the second; SP also recovers one input and HISP recovers neither. The constructed example exposes an identifiability failure: an edge can have zero marginal effect until another redundant edge is removed.

anchors.section: M. Automated Circuit Discovery and OR gates

method.core_idea: Represent a neural network as a researcher-chosen directed computational graph and automatically prune low-effect edges by activation patching, yielding a sparse task-conditioned subgraph for subsequent human interpretation.
method.mechanism: Given clean prompts x, corrupted prompts x', the full graph G, and threshold tau, ACDC begins with H=G and visits nodes from output to input. It tentatively removes each incoming edge, replaces every removed edge's clean activation with its cached activation on x', and evaluates the resulting subgraph by mean KL divergence from G (or a task-specific alternative). If deleting the candidate edge increases the score by less than tau, the deletion becomes permanent. The study adapts Subnetwork Probing to learn activation-interpolation masks and HISP to rank heads/components, then sweeps each method's sparsity control and scores overlap with manual or Tracr circuits, behavior-versus-edge Pareto curves, and reset-network controls.
assumptions: The selected prompt set isolates one coherent behavior whose implementation can be represented as a relatively sparse subgraph.
The researcher-selected node and edge granularity is fine enough to express the relevant computation without making search infeasible.
Activations from corrupted prompts, or zeros in ablations, constitute meaningful interventions rather than out-of-distribution states that change unrelated computations.
A small change in the chosen local metric after one edge deletion implies that the edge is unnecessary in the final jointly pruned graph.
Reverse-topological greedy deletion finds a useful circuit despite redundancy, nonlinear interactions, and dependence on parent traversal order.
Manual circuits are sufficiently complete and specific to serve as binary edge/node ground truth for ROC analysis.
Low held-out divergence plus few edges is adequate evidence of circuit faithfulness, not merely task-specific behavioral equivalence.
Task distributions with tens to hundreds of prompts are representative enough to support mechanistic claims beyond those exact templates.

techniques.role: Greedily removes computational-graph edges whose patched deletion changes the selected metric by less than a threshold.
Caches corrupted-input activations and substitutes them on removed edges to measure task-conditioned causal effects.
Traverses the graph from outputs toward inputs so pruning recursively follows surviving upstream paths.
Learns differentiable masks between clean and corrupted activations as a global optimization baseline.
Ranks heads or other components by gradient-based importance as a pruning baseline.
Treats manually reported or compiler-known circuit membership as binary labels and evaluates recovery over sparsity sweeps.
Compares held-out subgraph divergence or task loss against retained edge count without requiring a canonical circuit.
Permutes learned head/MLP dimensions and checks whether discovery methods spuriously recover task-like subgraphs from a network lacking the learned behavior.

evaluations.setting: Five canonical transformer circuits (Docstring, Greater-Than, IOI, tracr-xproportion, tracr-reverse) with corrupted-activation patching and KL/L2 optimization
evaluations.metric: Edge-recovery ROC AUC over sparsity hyperparameters
evaluations.result: ACDC AUC is 0.982 on Docstring, 0.853 on Greater-Than, and 0.869 on IOI; it is poor on the two Tracr tasks under this corruption setup.
evaluations.baseline: HISP scores 0.805/0.693/0.789 and SP scores 0.937/0.806/0.823 on Docstring/Greater-Than/IOI

evaluations.setting: Same canonical circuits under alternative task-specific losses and zero ablation
evaluations.result: Task-loss ACDC drops to 0.461 on Greater-Than, 0.589 on IOI, and 0.200 on tracr-reverse; with zero ablation it reaches 1.000 on both Tracr circuits but only 0.539 on IOI KL recovery.
evaluations.baseline: For task-loss recovery, HISP is 0.706/0.836/0.577 and SP is 0.812/0.707/0.193 on Greater-Than/IOI/tracr-reverse; zero-ablation HISP reaches 0.792 on IOI

evaluations.setting: Induction behavior in a 2-layer, 8-head attention-only transformer using 40 filtered OpenWebText sequences of 300 tokens
evaluations.metric: Held-out KL divergence to the full model versus number of retained edges
evaluations.result: Above roughly 20 edges, ACDC supplies every point on the reported Pareto frontier and has a slight behavior-per-edge advantage under the tested setup.
evaluations.baseline: Adapted Subnetwork Probing and HISP under both corrupted and zero activations

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 Small Greater-Than circuit on 100 prompts
evaluations.metric: Recovered component types, edge count, probability-difference behavior, and KL fidelity
evaluations.result: The headline ACDC run retains 68 of roughly 32,000 edges and recovers all five manual component types; the implemented 262-edge canonical circuit itself obtains 72% probability difference versus the full model's 84% and KL 0.078.
evaluations.baseline: The hand-built circuit reconstructed from Hanna, Liu, and Variengien (2023)

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 Small IOI circuit on 50 prompts from one template
evaluations.metric: Manual head-class overlap and KL fidelity
evaluations.result: At tau=0.0575, all nine recovered heads are in the 26-head manual circuit and span three functional classes, but negative and previous-token heads are missed; lower tau recovers them with many undocumented heads. The 1,041-edge canonical implementation has KL 0.44.
evaluations.baseline: The manually reported IOI circuit of Wang et al. (2023)

evaluations.setting: Docstring completion circuit in a 4-layer attention-only transformer
evaluations.metric: KL divergence, mean correct-minus-wrong logit difference, and edge count
evaluations.result: ACDC at tau=0.005 retains 258 edges with KL 0.33/logit difference 0.58; tau=0.095 retains 34 edges with KL 1.2/logit difference -1.7; optimizing logit difference retains 98 edges with KL 0.67/logit difference 0.32.
evaluations.baseline: Full model (1,377 edges, logit difference 0.48), eight manual heads with all connections (464 edges, KL 0.83, logit -0.62), and a 37-edge reconstructed manual graph (KL 1.1, logit -1.6)

evaluations.setting: Toy one-layer transformer implementing a two-input OR gate
evaluations.metric: Recovery of the two ground-truth causal input edges
evaluations.result: ACDC and SP each retain only one of the two redundant inputs; HISP retains neither.

limitations: Author-stated: ACDC automates only circuit-edge search; choosing a behavior, dataset, metric, corruption, graph granularity, and the semantic explanation of components remain human tasks.
Author-stated: results are highly sensitive to the corruption distribution, zero versus corrupted activation replacement, metric, threshold, and edge traversal order.
Author-stated: optimizing one scalar metric can miss negative or supporting components that are part of a manually understood mechanism but harm that metric.
Author-stated: human-produced canonical circuits are incomplete and may contain extraneous edges, so ROC true/false labels are not reliable ground truth.
Author-stated: the search remains computationally costly because every candidate edge requires a patched hypothesis test; realistic graphs contain many edges.

Reviewer-identified: most language-model evidence is on GPT-2 Small or substantially smaller transformers and narrow, templated behaviors; the study does not demonstrate scaling to modern large models or open-ended tasks.
Reviewer-identified: task faithfulness is evaluated under the same style of clean/corrupted interventions that defines the circuit, risking circularity and distribution-specific equivalence.
Reviewer-identified: the strongest exact ground truth comes from tiny compiler-generated Tracr networks and does not validate recovery in learned, redundant, polysemantic systems.
Reviewer-identified: sparse output is not itself a human-understandable explanation; the gendered-pronoun case still requires manual forward-pass and path-patching verification.

Reviewer-identified: only small samples are used for some case studies (50 IOI prompts, 100 Greater-Than and pronoun prompts), with limited reporting of sampling variance or stability across prompt templates.
failure_modes: Redundant paths or OR-like nonlinear interactions have zero marginal importance until alternatives are removed, so greedy deletion returns an arbitrary incomplete mechanism.
An ill-chosen corrupted distribution can introduce activation artifacts or erase the wrong feature, reversing circuit rankings and recovered components.
Zero ablation can move activations off distribution; corrupted ablation can preserve confounding information or require task-specific positional corruption.
A threshold that yields a compact graph can omit supporting heads and destroy behavioral fidelity, while a lower threshold can recover them only with many false positives.
Traversal-order dependence allows two runs on the same model and data to select different representatives of redundant computation.
Coarse graph nodes merge position-specific or feature-specific roles; Docstring head 1.4's distinct positional functions cannot be separated at the selected granularity.
A circuit can match KL on a narrow prompt family while failing the same behavior on paraphrases, longer context, adversarial prompts, or other output metrics.
Manual-reference ROC can penalize a genuinely important newly found edge as a false positive and reward an unnecessary documented edge as a true positive.
Discovery methods can optimize sparse subgraphs even in reset networks, revealing that architecture and activation statistics alone can create apparent circuit signal.
reusable_insights: Treat behavior definition, graph abstraction, circuit search, and semantic verification as separate modules with separate evidence; automating one does not validate the others.
Always sweep and report corruption distributions, patch baselines, metrics, thresholds, graph granularities, and traversal orders rather than presenting one recovered circuit as canonical.
Use at least three validation axes jointly: overlap with known components, held-out behavioral fidelity versus sparsity, and negative controls such as reset or random networks.
Report the full fidelity-sparsity frontier because a visually compelling minimal graph can have much worse task behavior than a larger recovered subgraph.
Exact or semi-synthetic circuits are valuable calibration fixtures, but they should complement rather than replace evaluations on learned networks with redundancy and superposition.
Test group and conditional importance, not only one-edge marginal effects, whenever redundant paths or nonlinear gates are plausible.
Preserve disagreement between the recovered circuit and manual reference as an audit target: it may expose either an algorithmic miss or an error in the supposed ground truth.
A discovery tool should emit intervention provenance alongside every edge: task distribution, clean/corrupted pairing, metric, ablation value, threshold, traversal order, and software/model version.
open_questions: Can circuit discovery optimize a multi-metric behavioral specification that retains both helpful and behavior-harming components without simply expanding to the full model?
How can search recover redundant, synergistic, or conditional groups of edges without exponential subset testing?
Which corruption-generation procedure yields interventions that are both on-manifold and causally targeted, and how can that choice be validated independently of circuit recovery?
Can discovered circuits be certified for paraphrases, prompt families, or continuous activation regions rather than one finite dataset?
How stable are recovered subgraphs across seeds, model checkpoints, equivalent graph factorizations, parent orders, and modest changes to tau?
What benchmark can provide realistic learned transformers with complete causal ground truth, including redundant and polysemantic mechanisms?
Can a scalable method jointly discover a sparse circuit and produce falsifiable semantic hypotheses for each component without relying on extensive human follow-up?
How should two behaviorally equivalent but structurally different circuits be scored when the model implements redundant algorithms?

competitive_landscape.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct successor and efficiency competitor from an overlapping author team
competitive_landscape.difference: Edge Attribution Patching linearly approximates the activation-patching effect of every edge with two forward passes and one backward pass, then ranks edges globally. It reports higher average circuit-recovery AUC than ACDC and is far cheaper than one patched forward evaluation per edge, but its first-order approximation can degrade for large perturbations and does not remove dependence on the task metric or corruption baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: InterpBench: Semi-Synthetic Transformers for Evaluating Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
competitive_landscape.relationship: Benchmark that directly addresses ACDC's unreliable manual-circuit ground truth
competitive_landscape.difference: InterpBench uses Strict Interchange Intervention Training to produce more realistic transformers whose intended circuits are known and whose non-circuit nodes are prevented from influencing output, then evaluates circuit-discovery methods. ACDC instead reconstructs tiny Tracr graphs or treats human analyses as truth; InterpBench improves validation realism but is a benchmark/training construction rather than a discovery algorithm.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 / NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks, 2025-10-11

competitive_landscape.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
competitive_landscape.difference: EAP-GP replaces a fixed integrated-gradient path with an adaptive GradPath intended to avoid zero-gradient and saturation regions. It evaluates six tasks through GPT-2 XL and reports faithfulness improvements up to 17.7%, extending scale beyond ACDC; it remains attribution- and patching-dependent and does not itself establish semantic completeness or corruption-invariant circuits.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering Transformer Circuits via a Hybrid Attribution and Pruning Framework
competitive_landscape.relationship: Hybrid approach that explicitly trades attribution speed against pruning faithfulness
competitive_landscape.difference: HAP first uses fast Edge Attribution Patching to restrict the candidate graph, then performs edge pruning on that subgraph. It reports a 46% speedup without losing tested faithfulness and preserves IOI S-inhibition components that pure attribution can drop. ACDC performs expensive greedy pruning over the full graph; HAP is more scalable but inherits shortlist-recall risk and its evidence is narrower than ACDC's six-task study.

competitive_landscape.title: Formal Mechanistic Interpretability: Automated Circuit Discovery with Provable Guarantees
competitive_landscape.relationship: Verification-based alternative to heuristic circuit recovery
competitive_landscape.difference: The formal approach uses neural-network verification to certify input-domain agreement, robustness under continuous patching perturbations, and notions of circuit minimality. This directly targets ACDC's finite-sample, threshold-sensitive evidence, but experiments focus on vision models where verification is tractable rather than GPT-scale language-model circuits.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim to systematize the recurring mechanistic-interpretability workflow, introduce ACDC to automate the edge-discovery stage, adapt two pruning methods to the same problem, and provide quantitative recovery metrics plus qualitative rediscovery of known circuits.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Across six behaviors, ACDC recovers high-overlap subgraphs, including all five Greater-Than component types in a 68-edge GPT-2 Small subgraph, exact Tracr circuits with zero ablation, competitive canonical-circuit AUC, and a novel pronoun-completion hypothesis later checked by practitioners.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the formalization of circuit discovery as an evaluable, automatable graph-search problem and the open implementation, not a generally reliable mechanistic oracle. The full-text ablations already show that ACDC is greedy, intervention-dependent, order-sensitive, and unable to resolve redundancy; later attribution, hybrid, benchmark, and verification work directly targets those weaknesses. It is best treated as a seminal search baseline and workflow scaffold whose outputs are hypotheses requiring independent semantic and behavioral validation.
